newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSURERS TO FORM NEW FIRM TO LIQUIDATE NISSAN LIFE.
newsitem.headline: INSURERS TO FORM NEW FIRM TO LIQUIDATE NISSAN LIFE.

text.p: The Life Insurance Association of Japan said on Friday that life insurers will establish a new company to liquidate Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co, as part of a framework to deal with huge losses at the failed firm.
Under the scheme, the new company will take over Nissan Life's policies and manage them until they mature, the association said.
The insurer's actual liabilities exceed its assets by around 300 billion yen, larger than the earlier estimate of 200 billion yen, it said.
The Policyholders Protection Fund, comprised of contributions from life insurers, will inject 200 billion yen into the new company.

The Finance Ministry on April 25 ordered Nissan Life to halt all operations except for servicing existing customers, as the insurer suffered heavy losses through excessive stock and real estate investments in the late 1980s "bubble era" of inflated asset prices.
It was the first failure of a life insurance firm in post-war Japan.
The Life Insurance Association has been serving as an interim caretaker for Nissan Life since its failure.

Kenjiro Hata, chairman of the association, told reporters that the association would continue asking Hitachi Ltd and Nissan Motor Co Ltd to offer support for the scheme by hiring Nissan Life employees and by refraining from cancelling policies they hold with the insurer.
Hitachi and Nissan Motor, Nissan Life's two largest clients, have rejected the association's requests to assist Nissan Life's restructuring, a senior association official said.
The senior official said the new company will cover the remaining 100 billion yen in Nissan Life's liabilities over the next five years through its profits.
He said that, under the framework developed by the association, the new company taking over Nissan Life's policies will cut the guaranteed return to policyholders to 2.75 percent.
Nearly half of Nissan Life's assets consist of policies held by individuals that guarantee a return of 5.5 percent, according to industry sources.

Commitments to policies with high returns have damaged the company's financial stability, and by cutting returns to 2.75 percent, the new company will be profitable, a senior official of the insurers' association told Friday's news conference.
"We conducted various simulations when we drew up the (Nissan Life) scheme and we believe the new company will not fail," the official said.
He did not give any estimates of annual profits for the new company.

"It is not known how many policies will be cancelled by Nissan Life's policyholders, so it is difficult to say how much profit the new company can post, although we have calculated various estimates," he said.
